text:
This paper looks at how to solve text classification problems efficiently [P2_p1_c02]. Traditional methods can struggle to generalize when there are many possible output categories and very few examples for some of them [P2_p1_c04]. 

The main idea is a text classifier called fastText [P2_p1_c02]. It treats text as a collection of words, averages those word representations, and feeds them into a linear classifier [P2_p1_c04]. To capture local word order without high computational costs, it uses a bag of n-grams as extra features [P2_p2_c03]. 

Regarding speed and cost, fastText is many orders of magnitude faster for training and evaluation than deep learning classifiers [P2_p1_c02]. It can train on more than one billion words in less than ten minutes using a standard multicore CPU [P2_p1_c02]. It can also classify half a million sentences among 312K classes in less than a minute [P2_p1_c02]. 

As for accuracy, fastText is often on par with deep learning classifiers [P2_p1_c02]. On sentiment analysis tasks, its accuracy is slightly better than some existing methods like char-CNN and char-CRNN, though a bit worse than VDCNN [P2_p3_c02]. Adding bigram information improves performance by 1 to 4 percent [P2_p3_c02]. 

The limitations noted in the paper include the fact that fastText does not use pre-trained word embeddings, which can explain small differences in accuracy compared to certain other approaches [P2_p3_c02].
